c699447383d5f5cca389a46a88a1164a53bf5b97.source:
Creating new things requires you to go to unexpected places. Radical ideas that give birth to new technologies tend to come from high-risk, out-of-distribution efforts. They reject conformity, taxonomies, and existing categories because the thing being created does not yet fit inside them.

This creates a problem when a new technology becomes a boom. Technological booms contain a paradox. They are born from ways of thinking that they eventually make less common. A boom begins as exploration and matures into exploitation. Exploration searches for something that does not yet have a name. Exploitation then makes what has been discovered into something safe, legible, obvious and repeatable to many people.

This is necessary for a technology to spread. A boom naturally attracts a larger number of people, and if the average person is risk-averse, the opportunity must become obvious enough for them to understand and bet on. But as the market grows, the thinking that created the market becomes less common within it. The technology succeeds while at the same time the force that shaped the discovery gets flattened by in-distribution thinking.

That is the curse of a technological boom: if the boom succeeds, what made it possible in the first place most likely will become less commonplace.

In Inheritance, Harvey Whitehouse argues that humanity has been shaped by three main biases: conformism, religiosity, and tribalism. The natural human tendency to avoid change is deeply ingrained in our survival instincts. If change gets exponentially faster as technology and AI advances faster, conformity and tribalism will grow as collective and individual defense mechanisms to adapt to change.

A successful boom activates the instinct of conformism and tribalism. Once a technology becomes high status, people begin to define what it is, how it works, and what does belongs inside it or not. The boom becomes a category. The category becomes a taxonomy. The taxonomy becomes a plan.

Taxonomies are where ideas go to die because it gives a false impression of arrival. The biggest challenge in an organization that continuously innovates is to preserve the way of thinking that made the discovery possible in the first place. This means going to unexpected places and questioning the plan instead of merely executing it. Rewriting the plan of the world.

This is why long-term thinking can be a major competitive strategy. The further into the future you look, the fewer established categories there are to tell you what should exist and therefore the more opportunities to create and discover.

Signs of unexplored creativity and long-term opportunity are often the same. You don’t have a name for what you are doing. It might feel like a toy. Traditionalists insist that this is not how things work. Most people don’t get it at first.

None of this means you are right. Most out-of-distribution ideas are bad. But every genuinely new idea must initially appear out of distribution. This means only that you may be somewhere the category has not yet reached. But if you succeed you might create a boom. And then another. And another.
c699447383d5f5cca389a46a88a1164a53bf5b97.zh:
创造新事物需要你到达意想不到的地方。催生新技术的激进想法往往来自高风险、分布外的努力。它们拒绝从众、拒绝分类、拒绝现有范畴，因为正在创造的东西还无法装入其中。

这就带来了一个问题：当一项新技术变成热潮时。技术热潮内含一个悖论——它诞生于一种思维方式，而这种思维方式最终会被热潮本身稀释。热潮始于探索，成熟于开采。探索寻找的是尚无名字的东西；开采则将已发现的东西变得安全、可读、显而易见、可被大量复制。

这对技术的传播是必要的。热潮自然会吸引更多人参与，如果普通人厌恶风险，机会必须足够明显，他们才能理解并押注。但随着市场扩大，创造市场的那种思维在市场内部反而越来越少。技术成功了，而推动发现的力量却被分布内思维碾平。

这就是技术热潮的诅咒：如果热潮成功，最初使之成为可能的东西很可能不再普遍。

在《Inheritance》一书中，Harvey Whitehouse 指出人类被三种主要偏见塑造：从众、宗教性和部落主义。人类避免变化的天性深植于生存本能。如果随着技术和 AI 的指数级加速，变化越来越快，从众和部落主义将作为个体和集体的防御机制而增长，以应对变化。

一场成功的潮热激活了从众和部落的本能。一旦某项技术获得高地位，人们就会开始定义它是什么、如何运作、什么属于它、什么不属于。热潮变成一个类别，类别变成分类体系，分类体系变成计划。

分类体系是创意的坟场，因为它给人一种已经到达的假象。在持续创新的组织中，最大的挑战是保留最初让发现成为可能的那种思维方式。这意味着要走向意想不到的地方，质疑计划而不是仅仅执行它。重写世界的蓝图。

这就是为什么长期思维可以成为一项重大竞争战略。你看得越远，既有的分类就越少，告诉你什么应该存在的东西就越少，因此创造和发现的机会就越多。

未开发的创造力信号和长期机会的信号往往是同一个：你做的事还没有名字；它可能看起来像个玩具；传统主义者坚称这不是常规做法；大多数人一开始看不懂。

这些都不意味着你是对的。大多数分布外的想法是错的。但每一个真正的新想法最初必然显得不在分布之内。这只意味着你可能处于分类尚未触及的地方。但如果你成功了，你也许会掀起一场热潮，然后又是一场，再来一场。

We scaled a robot model natively to 8,000 timesteps of context, 5 minutes worth of muscle memory, with constant inference cost. Robot policies used to live their lives a few frames at a time (< 0.1 sec), instantly forgetting what just happened. We pushed to 3 orders of magnitude beyond SOTA. 

Introducing RoboTTT. Test-Time Training (“TTT”) carries a tiny model *inside* the model. Every incoming sensor reading triggers one gradient step on that tiny core, so the history keeps getting compressed into its weights. The hidden state has a fixed size (literally a small neural net), so the robot can “grok” arbitrarily long experience with little overhead. Learning continues indefinitely after deployment.

We can then put an entire video in context as prompt! RoboTTT enables one-shot in-context learning from human video: in circuit board assembly, a human demonstrates a never-seen configuration once, and the robot imitates it faithfully. 

Humans drop things all the time, but we pick them up so fast that we don’t even notice. That reflex to fix is half of our physical competence. RoboTTT shows self-improvement on the fly: the robot is skilled at recovering from its own errors mid-episode, and each fix enters its context to inform the next move. The TTT core distills a general-purpose, failure-to-correction mapping from the training data.

One more thing. What excites me the most is a new Context Scaling Curve: from 128 to 8K timesteps, closed-loop performance hill-climbs steadily with no sign of saturation. 8K-context pretraining beats 1K by 62%. What LLM enjoys, robotics should too. Soon, even 1M context is not a fantasy.

1b2904406cccbc1dfb12872d934160b7c7d99cf4.zh:
我们将一个机器人模型原生扩展至 8,000 个时间步的上下文——相当于 5 分钟的肌肉记忆，且推理成本恒定。过去的机器人策略只能活在几帧之内（< 0.1 秒），转瞬即忘。我们将这一指标推到了 SOTA 的三个数量级以上。

推出 RoboTTT。Test-Time Training（"TTT"）在模型*内部*携带一个微型模型。每一次传感器读数都会在这个微型核心上触发一次梯度更新，历史信息由此不断被压缩进它的权重中。隐状态大小固定（本质上就是一个小型神经网络），因此机器人能以极低开销"领悟"任意长度的经验。部署后学习无限持续。

我们甚至可以将整段视频放入上下文中作为提示！RoboTTT 支持从人类视频中进行一次性上下文学习：在电路板组装中，人类演示一次从未见过的配置，机器人即可忠实复现。

人类总是掉东西，但我们捡得如此之快以至于自己都察觉不到。这种修正反射构成了我们身体能力的一半。RoboTTT 展示了运行中的自我提升：机器人善于在任务中途从自身错误中恢复，每次修正都会进入上下文以指导下一步动作。TTT 核心从训练数据中蒸馏出一个通用的"失败→纠正"映射。

还有一件事。最让我兴奋的是一条新的上下文扩展曲线：从 128 到 8K 时间步，闭环性能持续攀升，毫无饱和迹象。8K 上下文预训练比 1K 高出 62%。LLM 享有的，机器人学也应当享有。不久的将来，即便 1M 上下文也并非幻想。

I'm glad people still understand the importance of building high-quality retrieval systems in 2026, especially as the outer models/harnesses are getting better every day.

Making agentic retrieval work in production  doesn't necessarily require groundbreaking new techniques around retrieval or planning. This article shows that you do need to spend engineering time tuning chunking, synchronization, reranking, tool API design, permissioning, and more. Some interesting tidbits:
* Concatenating onto existing Slack threads as one contiguous chunk with heuristics for determining additional relevant context
* Real-time updates for Slack
* Separate chunking/updates for codebases
* The discovery that hybrid search works well (not like this was a super new realization, but always good to validate and understand the specific parameters they tweaked) 
* Having natural guardrails on which data sources are relevant for which projects

Building simple retrieval is easy, building production retrieval is hard. We had to deal with a lot of these challenges when productionizing our own Index feature within LlamaParse.
50ce0134d128cd2c257a3663ed000eb793d50ae6.zh:
很高兴看到 2026 年人们仍然理解构建高质量检索系统的重要性，尤其是在外层模型和 harness 每天都在变得更好的情况下。

让 agentic retrieval 在生产环境中真正可用，并不一定需要在检索或规划上采用突破性新技术。这篇文章表明，你确实需要投入工程时间来调优分块、同步、重排序、工具 API 设计、权限控制等。几个有意思的细节：
* 将现有 Slack 线程拼接成一个连续块，并用启发式方法判断额外相关上下文
* Slack 的实时更新
* 针对代码库采用独立的分块和更新机制
* 发现混合搜索效果不错（这并不是什么特别新的认知，但验证并理解他们具体调过的参数总是有价值的）
* 对哪些数据源与哪些项目相关设置自然的护栏

构建简单检索很容易，构建生产级检索很难。我们在将自己的 LlamaParse Index 功能产品化时，也不得不处理很多这类挑战。

AI is one of the few truly general-purpose technologies, which means it can be shaped into almost anything we want it to be. It’s a kind of technological Rorschach test. Models are so malleable that we project onto them all of our views, hopes, and fears. In that sense, AI often becomes a reflection of ourselves. It's a mirror. Not of what it actually is but of yourself.

If you are generally paranoid or fearful, you will project that into AI. If you are generally optimistic, you are more likely to see AI as an opportunity. That is part of why it is so controversial: it can appear to be almost anything, depending on the worldview you bring to it.
2bf57f1ec92705e42e0e14ac7b9effd06fac33e1.zh:
AI 是少数真正的通用技术之一，这意味着它几乎可以被塑造成我们想要的任何样子。它就像一种技术版的罗夏测试。模型具有极强的可塑性，以至于我们会把自己的观点、希望和恐惧都投射到它们身上。从这个意义上说，AI 往往成了我们自身的映照。它是一面镜子，映出的不是它本来的样子，而是你自己。

如果你通常多疑或恐惧，你就会把这种情绪投射到 AI 上。如果你通常乐观，就更可能把 AI 视为一种机会。这也是它如此有争议的部分原因：它会呈现出几乎任何样子，取决于你带着怎样的世界观来看它。

This is awesome. Instead of doing work this morning, I spent some time brushing up on math to provide a handwavy overview to anyone else who like me doesn't have a math background and is rusty: 

At a distance, the conjecture is basically that if a n-dimensional polynomial function (e.g. F(x, y, z) map to some output (x', y', z')) meets some special conditions, then 1) it is invertible, and 2) the inverse is polynomial. 

Disproving the conjecture requires finding a n-dimensional polynomial function that meets these special conditions, but is either 1) not invertible at all, or 2) is invertible but not polynomial. (2) is actually not a possibility due to some other math theorem - if there is an inverse, the inverse has to be polynomial. 

Invertibility just means the function can be "undone" at every single input point - if input (x1, y1, z1) maps to output (x2, y2, z2), then output (x2, y2, z2) can map to input (x1, y1, z1). A function is not invertible if multiple input points (x, y, z)'s map to the same output (x, y, z)

Here Fable 5 presumably did some search and found a function that was not invertible. 

That function is this:  
F(x, y, z) = (
z(1+xy)^3 + y^2(1+xy)(4+3xy),
y+3x(1+xy)^2z + 3xy^2(4+3xy),
2x-3x^2y-x^3z
)

This function meets the special conditions (jacobian determinant is a non-zero constant for every point), but has multiple input points that map to the same output: 

Inputs: (0, 0, -1/4), (1, -3/2, 13/2), and (-1, 3/2, 13/2)
all map to the same output: (-1/4, 0, 0)

-----

The Jacobian is the multivariable version of a derivative, so it is a function of a specific input point. When the Jacobian determinant is non-zero at a specific input point, there is local invertibility around that point. This conjecture was stronger in that if it was non-zero (and constant, due to being over the complex numbers, which I don't quite get and I ran out of time to understand), then the function is globally invertible. 

-----

What's interesting here is that finding counterexamples seem like the type of math work that agentic models excel at. It involves generating and crawling a large search space, using priors to narrow it down, and a bit of brute force and raw compute power. Machines can process a wide set of possibilities faster than humans, which is helpful for finding counterexamples.

从远处看，这个猜想基本上是说，如果一个 n 维多项式函数（例如 F(x, y, z) 映射到某个输出 (x', y', z')）满足一些特殊条件，那么 1) 它是可逆的，2) 它的逆也是多项式。

要证伪这个猜想，需要找到一个满足这些特殊条件的 n 维多项式函数，但它要么 1) 完全不可逆，要么 2) 可逆但逆不是多项式。由于另一个数学定理，(2) 实际上不可能：如果存在逆，那么这个逆必须是多项式。

可逆性只是指函数在每一个输入点都可以被“撤销”：如果输入 (x1, y1, z1) 映射到输出 (x2, y2, z2)，那么输出 (x2, y2, z2) 可以映射回输入 (x1, y1, z1)。如果多个输入点 (x, y, z) 映射到同一个输出 (x, y, z)，这个函数就不可逆。

这里 Fable 5 大概是做了一些搜索，找到了一个不可逆函数。

这个函数是：
F(x, y, z) = (
z(1+xy)^3 + y^2(1+xy)(4+3xy),
y+3x(1+xy)^2z + 3xy^2(4+3xy),
2x-3x^2y-x^3z
)

这个函数满足特殊条件（Jacobian determinant 在每个点都是非零常数），但有多个输入点会映射到同一个输出：

输入：(0, 0, -1/4)、(1, -3/2, 13/2) 和 (-1, 3/2, 13/2)
全部映射到同一个输出：(-1/4, 0, 0)

-----

Jacobian 是导数的多变量版本，因此它是某个特定输入点的函数。当 Jacobian determinant 在某个特定输入点非零时，该点附近存在局部可逆性。这个猜想更强，它认为如果它非零（并且由于是在复数域上所以是常数，这点我还没完全理解，也没时间继续搞懂），那么这个函数就是全局可逆的。

-----

这里有趣的是，寻找反例看起来正是 agentic models 擅长的数学工作类型。它涉及生成并爬梳一个巨大的搜索空间，利用先验来缩小范围，再加上一点暴力搜索和原始算力。机器能比人类更快处理大量可能性，这对寻找反例很有帮助。

what's the difference between a loop and a graph? (marketing edition)

both are ways to run an agent, the difference is who decides the path, the agent or you.

a loop still starts with you. you set the goal, the brief, and the bar it has to clear. what the agent owns is the path.

take writing an SEO article: hand it the brief and it drafts, reads the draft back against that brief, rewrites the weak parts, checks again, and keeps circling until it clears the bar. the one thing you did not write is the step-by-step it took to get there.

a graph is you drawing the steps and the routes between them ahead of time. same article, but now you set the map: research the keyword and the competitors ranking for it. draft from what you find. score that draft against your rubric.

if it clears, add the internal links and publish. if it misses, back to the draft. the agent still decides how to handle each step, it just travels the routes you laid down.

the shape of this has a name, a state machine. every node is a state the work can be in, and a check at each one decides where it goes next, forward when it clears or back to an earlier node when it misses.

if you have built a workflow in n8n, you have already drawn one. nodes wired together, branches that fire on a condition, a step that loops until it clears, that picture is a graph. an agent graph is the same shape, the nodes hold agents doing the work instead of single api calls.

the way I think about it, a graph is a map of loops and checkpoints. some nodes run once, others are their own loop where the agent works something out, and the checkpoints between them read the result and route the work. you keep laying down nodes and checkpoints until the map reliably gives you the output you want.

the vault accelerator I run at my agency is one of these maps, 3 sessions that hand off in a fixed order:

> research session: reads our company brain and past campaign results, pulls in competitor and market context, and builds the cohort we go after
> landing page session: takes that research and builds the page from it
> content session: uses the research and the page to write the copy, illustrations, and slides for the live sessions we run

inside the content session runs a loop, a critic scores each draft against a rubric and sends it back until it clears the bar. that is one node on the map, the checkpoints between the sessions carry the work from one to the next

a graph earns its extra setup on anything you run every week:

> validation gates the work cannot skip
> a fixed set of routes the job can take
> a clear failure point, you see the exact step something broke on

a loop on its own is enough for the work you only do once, where you don't know the path yet, let the agent find it. graphs earn their place on the jobs you repeat, the content pipeline, the SEO and AEO funnel step by step, the vault accelerator

once the map works you reuse it, feed it the next cohort and the whole pipeline runs again

past the loop, the next thing you design is the map it runs inside.

循环和图有什么区别？（营销版）

两者都是运行智能体的方式，区别在于路径由谁决定：智能体，还是你。

循环仍然从你开始。你设定目标、简报和必须达到的标准。智能体负责的是路径。

以写一篇 SEO 文章为例：你把简报交给它，它会起草、对照简报回读草稿、重写薄弱部分、再次检查，并不断循环，直到达到标准。你唯一没有写的是它达成目标所走的具体步骤。

图则是你提前画好步骤，以及步骤之间的路线。同样是那篇文章，但现在由你设定地图：研究关键词和排名靠前的竞争对手。根据发现起草。按你的评分标准评估草稿。

如果达标，就添加内部链接并发布。如果没达标，就回到草稿。智能体仍然决定如何处理每一步，只是沿着你铺好的路线前进。

这种结构有个名字，叫状态机。每个节点都是工作可能处于的一种状态，每个节点上的检查决定下一步去哪里：达标就前进，没达标就退回到前面的节点。

如果你在 n8n 里搭过工作流，其实你已经画过一个了。节点连接在一起，分支按条件触发，某个步骤循环直到达标，那张图就是一个图。智能体图也是同样的形态，只是节点里放的是执行工作的智能体，而不是单个 api 调用。

我的理解是，图就是循环和检查点的地图。有些节点只运行一次，另一些节点本身就是一个循环，智能体会在里面把事情处理好；节点之间的检查点读取结果并路由工作。你不断铺设节点和检查点，直到这张地图能稳定产出你想要的结果。

我在机构里运行的 vault accelerator 就是这样一张地图，由 3 个按固定顺序交接的 session 组成：

> research session：读取我们的公司大脑和过往活动结果，引入竞争对手和市场背景，并构建我们要触达的人群
> landing page session：接收研究结果，并据此构建页面
> content session：利用研究结果和页面，撰写我们直播 session 所需的文案、插图和幻灯片

content session 内部运行着一个循环，评论器会按评分标准评估每版草稿，并把它退回去，直到达标。这是地图上的一个节点；session 之间的检查点把工作从一个环节带到下一个环节。

图在你每周都要运行的事情上值得投入额外设置：

> 工作不能跳过的验证门
> 任务可以走的一组固定路线
> 清晰的失败点，你能看到到底是哪一步出了问题

对于只做一次、你还不知道路径的工作，单独一个循环就够了，让智能体自己找到路径。图适用于重复性的任务：内容流水线、SEO 和 AEO 漏斗的逐步推进、vault accelerator。

一旦地图跑通，你就可以复用它，输入下一批人群，整条流水线再次运转。

越过循环之后，你要设计的下一个东西，就是它运行其中的那张地图。

Wikis are pure slop

Pure slop is LLM content from summaries / groups of other LLM content in a big sloppy mess using other peoples prompts built for generic projects (my definition).

It's my current belief that if you want to do analysis of large scale unstructured documents with AI today, you currently need constrained pipelines with steps that were verified by a domain expert in the loop.

DocETL from @sh_reya has gotten a lot easier to use since I used it last. It's skill guides you through building your own AI enabled ETL pipelines and helps you verify after each step - it also handles all of the LLM caching and helps you test with multiple LLMs.

If you want to build a Wiki for your repo, there are lots of good learnings from slop cannon wiki builders, but I'm of the belief that if you're introducing a wiki, you probably should understand, tune and verify how it was produced.
f9aa35960f4e9461d28c7a90f7cf8077076fdbd7.zh:
Wiki 纯粹是垃圾内容

所谓纯垃圾内容，是指由其他 LLM 内容的摘要/集合拼成的一大团混乱内容，还用了别人为通用项目写的提示词（我的定义）。

我目前认为，如果你今天想用 AI 分析大规模非结构化文档，就需要受约束的流水线，并且每一步都要有领域专家参与验证。

@sh_reya 的 DocETL 比我上次使用时好用多了。它的 skill 会引导你构建自己的 AI 驱动 ETL 流水线，并帮助你在每一步之后进行验证；它还会处理所有 LLM 缓存，并帮助你用多个 LLM 进行测试。

如果你想为自己的仓库构建 Wiki，那些垃圾内容生成器式的 Wiki 构建工具里确实有很多值得学习的地方，但我认为，如果你要引入 Wiki，就应该理解、调优并验证它是如何生成的。

5f163240c474b133931f828fa6268af51f5a54cf.source: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
5f163240c474b133931f828fa6268af51f5a54cf.zh: 我发现和 LLM 协作时，一个很有用的方法是来一段长时间的随口碎碎念。有时 LLM 需要更多信息才能理解你想实现什么，但你又懒得打字。这种情况下，我喜欢往后一靠，切到 /voice，然后随便说上大概 10 分钟，乱七八糟也没关系，想到什么说什么。有时我会一开始先说明，比如“切到语音识别了，有错别字请见谅……”。有时我会把它变成几轮小采访。但我发现，LLM 不知怎么很擅长重构这种又长又不连贯的碎碎念，而且它复述出来的你那团乱麻般的想法，往往比你一开始说的清晰不少。结果就是你们之间的心智同步会更好，之后需要纠正的地方也会少很多。

very notable trajectory comparison writeup here buried in the RLM paper from @a1zhang and @lateinteraction.

an open secret of "frontier" model training is that even without training on test, you can basically cheat by training on test lookalikes, enabling you to goalseek almost any benchmark number you want.

however when they are released open weights, 99% of the time the norm is that you do not get the datasets/rlenvs that would easily show you if someone was training on Temu Tbench, so there is plausible deniability. Alex and Omar discuss applying standard NLP distance metrics on hidden trajectories. There's no ultimate solution here, but they have some prelim explorations. It happens to support the finding that RLMs can generalize to unseen tasks that share latent structure observed in training.

ddbd63e144ce73c1258f698c3f71b4ebb63d4faa.source:
Transformers struggle to generalize to tasks they were not explicitly trained on. Instead, we propose in 2026 that it is the job of the harness to generalize through composition.

We observe a powerful property when training RLMs: for tasks with shared structure that look different, the root model naturally learns the same trajectory, meaning it views the two task trajectories as the same! In other words, the Transformer does not need additional generalization capabilities to transfer capabilities from one task to the other, the harness induces it.

We find that well-designed harnesses form a quotient set over task trajectories, meaning their individual LLM calls can see structurally “similar” tasks as near-identical, token-for-token! Harnesses can effectively generalize for the Transformer during training, without relying on any intrinsic generalization capability from the model.

For example, RLMs can see problems of different lengths as the same: we show that RLMs can train exclusively on short tasks, and fully generalize to similar but unseen tasks 8-32x longer because it produces near identical trajectories for both.

Taking this further, we show that tasks across different domains (e.g. math solutions vs. essay writing) that share a decomposition strategy exhibit the same generalization effect. RLMs can train on the problem of finding which essays belong to the same author and improve performance on finding math problems that share similar solutions.

The full blogpost, experiments, and discussion are in the thread below.
ddbd63e144ce73c1258f698c3f71b4ebb63d4faa.zh:
Transformers 难以泛化到没有被显式训练过的任务。因此，我们在 2026 年提出：泛化应当由 harness 通过组合来完成。

在训练 RLM 时，我们观察到一个强大的性质：对于共享结构但表面不同的任务，根模型会自然学到相同的轨迹，也就是说，它会把这两类任务轨迹视为相同！换句话说，Transformer 不需要额外的泛化能力，就能把能力从一个任务迁移到另一个任务，是 harness 诱导了这种迁移。

我们发现，设计良好的 harness 会在任务轨迹上形成一个商集，这意味着其单个 LLM 调用可以把结构上“相似”的任务视为几乎完全相同，甚至逐 token 近似一致！在训练期间，harness 可以有效替 Transformer 完成泛化，而不依赖模型自身的内在泛化能力。

例如，RLM 可以把不同长度的问题视为相同：我们展示了 RLM 只用短任务训练，也能完全泛化到相似但未见过、长度为 8-32 倍的任务，因为它会为两者生成几乎相同的轨迹。

更进一步，我们展示了不同领域的任务（例如数学解题 vs. 文章写作）只要共享一种分解策略，也会表现出同样的泛化效果。RLM 可以在“判断哪些文章出自同一作者”这个问题上训练，并提升在“寻找具有相似解法的数学题”任务上的表现。

great post by jeff! a few thoughts I had as I read along, wrt what we're building at langchain:

> design a compound learning machine

as you use or deploy agents, they need to be learning! high level, i believe traces are the core of this - you need to see what happened, get feedback on it, and then update the system

> own your context, rent your intelligence

agree with this sentiment - own your "tacit and institutional knowledge", make it easy to swap out models. i think the phrasing will get confusing tho - what exactly is intelligence? @satyanadella had a great post here (https://t.co/wq8z68YBVy) where he says a lot of things that agrees with this, but he also says stuff like "In consuming intelligence, you are creating intelligence... This is your particular intelligence". the nuance is there is general intelligence (eg the models, which you should rent) and then your company proprietary intelligence, which you should own. both could reasonably be called intelligence though, so its confusing

> build your tools, buy infra

buy the lowest common denominator infra, build specific things on top of it. at LC we try to focus on lowest common denominator infra (observability, deployment, sandboxes), but we can do better - we have some cool stuff coming in that regard

> develop rubrics

evals are important!

> store and learn from production traces

yup. was this article just an ad for langsmith all along? who knows!

当你使用或部署智能体时，它们需要持续学习！从高层看，我认为 traces 是核心：你需要看到发生了什么，获得反馈，然后更新系统。

认同这种观点：拥有你的“隐性知识和组织知识”，并让模型易于替换。不过我觉得这个表述可能会让人困惑：智能到底是什么？@satyanadella 在这里有一篇很棒的帖子（https://t.co/wq8z68YBVy），他说了很多与此一致的观点，但也说了类似“In consuming intelligence, you are creating intelligence... This is your particular intelligence”这样的话。微妙之处在于，存在通用智能（例如模型，你应该租用），也存在公司专有智能（你应该拥有）。但两者都可以合理地被称为智能，所以会有些混淆。
